issues.legal_issue: A government lessor may cancel and resume a lease when the grant permits re-entry for the lessor’s own use or a public purpose and that need exists.
material_facts: The lease and its renewal preserved a term allowing the State to resume the premises if required for its own use or a public purpose, subject to notice and provisions concerning the building on the land.
The State required the premises for extending the High Court and the office of the Advocate-General, and the Court treated that requirement as a public purpose.
The lease was renewed on the same terms, including the re-entry term; the State’s need had been considered before the renewal.
issues.conclusion: The cancellation and resumption order was valid and did not suffer from illegality.
issues.legal_principle: Sections 2 and 3 of the Government Grants Act, 1895, as amended in Uttar Pradesh by U.P. Act 13 of 1960, provide that government grants operate according to their terms notwithstanding contrary general law. Applying State of U.P. v. Zahoor Ahmad, AIR 1973 SC 2520, the Court held that the grant’s re-entry term governed and permitted resumption for the stated public purpose.

predicates.government_lease_resumption_dispute: A dispute concerns a government lessor’s cancellation of a lease and resumption of the leased premises.
predicates.grant_permits_reentry_for_public_need: The lease terms allow the government lessor to re-enter the premises when they are required for its own use or a public purpose.
predicates.public_need_established: The government lessor required the premises for a public project.

issues.definition: When a government lease permits re-entry for the lessor’s own use or a public purpose and that need is established, the lease cancellation and resumption are valid.

issues.legal_issue: Resuming leased land under a term also used for comparable government leases does not amount to discriminatory treatment merely because other land was acquired through a different process.
material_facts: The lessees argued that other land had been acquired under acquisition legislation with compensation and that the State had not previously resumed land in this manner.
The State showed that another leased government plot had been resumed under a similar lease term without acquisition proceedings, and that challenge to the resumption had been dismissed.
The other properties referred to by the lessees had been acquired at the request of a development authority for different projects.
issues.conclusion: The lessees could not establish an Article 14 violation on the basis of the asserted difference in treatment.
issues.legal_principle: The Court assessed the discrimination claim against the record of government action, noting that a similar resumption under a similar lease term had occurred before; the properties acquired through acquisition proceedings were acquired for different projects. It therefore rejected the claim of unequal treatment under Article 14 of the Constitution.

predicates.government_lease_resumption_dispute: A dispute concerns a government lessor’s resumption of leased premises.
predicates.prior_comparable_resumption_under_simila: The government had previously resumed another leased property under a similar contractual term without using acquisition proceedings.
predicates.comparison_acquisitions_concerned_differ: The properties relied on as comparators were acquired for projects different from the project for which the disputed premises were resumed.

issues.definition: In a government lease-resumption dispute, a prior comparable resumption under similar terms, alongside acquisition comparators involving different projects, does not establish discriminatory treatment.

issues.legal_issue: When a government grant prescribes a process for resuming leased premises and the lessor follows that process, possession may be recovered under the grant without separate proceedings under another law.
material_facts: The lease term prescribed written notice to the lessees and a period for removal of buildings before possession could be taken; it also addressed compensation if the lessor chose to purchase a building.
The State gave notice of resumption, considered and rejected the lessees’ objection, and tendered compensation for the building.
The High Court had held that the State could not take forcible possession and had to use a procedure established by another law.
The Supreme Court allowed the lessees three months to deliver possession and stated that the State could take forcible possession if they failed to do so.
issues.conclusion: The grant’s resumption process was sufficient, and no separate procedure under another law was required; the High Court’s contrary observation was set aside. If the lessees failed to surrender possession within the time allowed by the Court, the State could take forcible possession.
issues.legal_principle: Section 3 of the Government Grants Act, 1895, as amended in Uttar Pradesh, makes the terms of a government grant effective according to their tenor. Applying State of U.P. v. Zahoor Ahmad, AIR 1973 SC 2520, the Court held that the specific resumption process in the lease governed, and no additional procedure under another law was required where that process was followed.

predicates.government_lease_possession_dispute: A dispute concerns a government lessor’s recovery of possession of leased premises.
predicates.grant_specifies_resumption_process: The lease terms prescribe the notice and other steps required before the lessor may resume possession.
predicates.required_resumption_steps_followed: The government lessor gave the prescribed notice and followed the applicable steps for resumption, including addressing any required compensation for a building.

issues.definition: If a government lease-resumption dispute involves a grant that specifies the resumption process and the lessor follows that process, possession may be recovered under the grant without separate proceedings.
